decks.title: Production Function — Part 1: Inputs, Output, and Total, Average and Marginal Product
goals: Explain the production function and distinguish the short run from the long run
Calculate average and marginal product from a total product schedule, and total product from marginal products
Explain how total product and average product behave as marginal product changes

slides.heading: Production Function and Law of Variable Proportions
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how **inputs** turn into **output**, and the three measures of output: **total, average and marginal product**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: the production function, fixed and variable factors, short and long run, total, average and marginal product, and how they are related
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every producer, from a bakery in Shillong to a millet farm in Bastar, turns inputs into output. In this chapter we study that technical link. Part one defines the production function, separates fixed from variable factors, and builds three measures of output: total, average and marginal product.

slides.heading: What a production function is
slides.body_md:
A **production function** is the **technical relationship** between the **physical quantities of inputs** and the **maximum physical output**, for a **given technology**.

It is written **Q = f(L, K)**: output depends on labour and capital.

visual.alt: Flow of a production function: physical inputs of land, labour and capital, with a given technology, produce the maximum physical output
visual.caption: Q = f(L, K)

slides.narration: A production function tells us the most output a firm can get from given amounts of inputs, with the technology it has. It is purely physical. It talks about workers, machines and kilograms, not rupees. Prices and costs come later, when we study cost.

slides.heading: Fixed and variable factors
columns: A **fixed factor** cannot be changed quickly as output changes: buildings, heavy machines, land under a lease.
A **variable factor** can be changed within the period: workers, raw materials, power.

headers: Input at an imagined Bhagalpur silk shed
rows: Take months to buy and install

visual.alt: Table classifying inputs of an imagined Bhagalpur silk shed: looms and the shed are fixed in the short run because they cannot be changed quickly; weavers and silk yarn are variable

slides.narration: Some inputs take a long time to change. A silk shed cannot add looms or enlarge its building within weeks, so these are fixed factors. Weavers and yarn can be increased within days, so they are variable factors. Whether a factor is fixed depends on the length of the period we consider.

slides.heading: Quick check: which relationship?
slides.body_md: A Kanpur leather unit adds cutters to its six fixed cutting tables and watches output. What is it studying?
slides.narration: Count how many inputs are changing. If one input changes while the others stay fixed, which kind of production function is it?

slides.heading: Short run and long run
slides.body_md:
In the **short run** at least one factor is **fixed**; output changes only through the variable factor.

In the **long run** **all factors** can be varied.

rows: A second kiln with its own crew

visual.alt: Table comparing the short-run production function, where at least one factor is fixed and returns to a factor apply, with the long-run production function, where all factors vary and returns to scale apply

slides.narration: The short run is any period in which at least one factor is fixed. The firm can only change output by using more or less of its variable factors, so the proportion between factors changes. In the long run every input can change, even the size of the plant. The short run leads to returns to a factor; the long run leads to returns to scale.

slides.heading: Total, average and marginal product
slides.body_md:
- **Total product (TP):** total output of all units of the variable factor.
- **Average product (AP) = TP ÷ L.**
- **Marginal product (MP) = TPn − TPn−1:** the addition to TP from **one more unit**.

rows: Total output of all units of the variable factor
Output per unit of the variable factor
Addition to TP from one more unit

visual.alt: Table of total, average and marginal product: total product is total output and equals the sum of marginal products; average product is total product divided by units of labour; marginal product is the change in total product from one more unit

slides.narration: Total product is everything the variable factor produces with the fixed factor. Average product is output per worker: total product divided by the number of workers. Marginal product is the extra output from one more worker: the change in total product. Adding up all the marginal products gives total product.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a Nagpur packing shed
slides.body_md: Find MP and AP for an imagined Nagpur orange-packing shed with one shed and 1 to 6 workers.
bullets: Step 1 — MP = this TP minus the previous TP (12 − 0, 30 − 12, …).
Step 2 — AP = TP ÷ workers (12 ÷ 1, 30 ÷ 2, …).
Step 3 — Compare: AP rises while MP is above it.

visual.alt: Worked example table for an imagined Nagpur orange-packing shed: with 1 to 6 workers total product is 12, 30, 51, 68, 80, 84 crates, marginal product 12, 18, 21, 17, 12, 4 and average product 12, 15, 17, 17, 16, 14
visual.caption: Imagined figures: MP = change in TP; AP = TP ÷ workers.

slides.narration: Work down the table. The first worker adds twelve crates. Two workers pack thirty, so the second adds eighteen. Three pack fifty-one, so the third adds twenty-one. Average product is total crates divided by workers: twelve, fifteen, seventeen. While each new worker adds more than the average, the average rises.

slides.heading: Quick check: the fourth packer
slides.body_md: The shed packs 51 crates with 3 workers and 68 with 4. What is the marginal product of the fourth worker?
slides.narration: Marginal product is the change in total product when one more worker joins. Subtract.

slides.heading: The total product curve
slides.body_md: TP rises **at an increasing rate** up to **K** (point of inflexion), then **at a diminishing rate** up to its **maximum M**, and then **falls**.

slides.narration: Here is a smooth total product curve for an imagined millet farm with fixed land. At first the curve gets steeper: each worker adds more than the last. After point K it gets flatter: each worker adds less. At M the curve is flat, its maximum. After that, extra workers actually reduce output.

slides.heading: How TP depends on MP
slides.body_md: TP changes by the amount of MP, so the **sign and size of MP** decide the shape of TP.

visual.alt: Table linking marginal product to total product: rising MP makes TP rise at an increasing rate, maximum MP is the point of inflexion, falling positive MP makes TP rise at a diminishing rate, zero MP is TP maximum and negative MP makes TP fall

slides.narration: Total product changes by exactly the marginal product each time. So when marginal product is rising, total product rises faster and faster. When marginal product falls but stays positive, total product still rises, only more slowly. When marginal product is zero, total product is at its peak. When marginal product is negative, total product falls.

slides.heading: Quick check: does TP fall with MP?
slides.body_md: True or false? Total product starts falling as soon as marginal product starts falling.
slides.narration: Remember that total product changes by the amount of marginal product. If that amount is smaller but still positive, which way does total product move?

slides.heading: Average and marginal product curves
slides.body_md: MP **rises**, reaches a **peak**, **cuts AP at AP's maximum**, becomes **zero**, then **negative**. AP stays positive.

visual.caption: Imagined: MP = 18L − 3L², AP = 9L − L²; the horizontal axis is at zero, so negative MP lies below it.

slides.narration: Now look at average and marginal product for the same farm. Marginal product climbs to a peak at three workers, then falls. It crosses the average product curve exactly where average product is highest, at four and a half workers on this smooth curve. At six workers marginal product is zero, and after that it dips below the axis.

slides.heading: How AP depends on MP
slides.body_md: An addition **above** the average pulls the average **up**; an addition **below** it pulls the average **down**.

headers: Marginal product compared with average product
rows: Still positive while TP is positive

visual.alt: Table of the AP and MP relationship: when MP is above AP, AP rises; when they are equal AP is at its maximum; when MP is below AP, AP falls; MP can be negative while AP stays positive

slides.narration: Think of a cricketer's batting average. A score above the average raises it; a score below the average lowers it. In the same way, when marginal product is above average product, average product rises. When it is equal, average product is at its peak. When it is below, average product falls.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: from MP to TP at Thanjavur
slides.body_md: An imagined Thanjavur plot gets marginal products of 6, 10, 13, 9, 5, 2, 0 and −3 rows a day from eight labourers. Build total product.
bullets: Step 1 — TP is the running total of MP.
Step 2 — TP is highest (45) where MP becomes zero.
Step 3 — The negative MP of the eighth labourer makes TP fall to 42.

visual.alt: Worked example table for an imagined Thanjavur paddy plot: marginal products 6, 10, 13, 9, 5, 2, 0, -3 add up to total products 6, 16, 29, 38, 43, 45, 45, 42; TP is highest at 45 rows where MP is zero and falls when MP is negative
visual.caption: Imagined figures: TP is the running sum of MP.

slides.narration: To go from marginal to total product, keep a running total. Six, then six plus ten makes sixteen, plus thirteen makes twenty-nine, and so on. Total product peaks at forty-five rows when the seventh labourer adds nothing. The eighth labourer has a negative marginal product, so total product falls to forty-two.

slides.heading: Quick check: a brass artisan
slides.body_md: The next artisan at a Moradabad brass unit adds 14 vases; the average so far is 11. What happens to average product?
slides.narration: Is the new addition above or below the current average?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Some factors fixed versus all variable
AP = TP ÷ L; MP = change in TP
MP = 0 at TP maximum; MP = AP at AP maximum

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the production function, short and long run, the definitions of total, average and marginal product and their relationships

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. A production function is a physical link between inputs and output. In the short run some factors are fixed; in the long run all can change. Average product is output per unit and marginal product is the extra output from one more unit. Total product peaks where marginal product is zero, and average product peaks where marginal product equals it.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **MP = TPn − TPn−1** and **AP = TP ÷ L** before calculating; show each subtraction or division.
TP from MP: add the marginal products **cumulatively**.
Say **"TP rises at a diminishing rate"** when MP falls but is positive — not "TP falls".
Draw AP and MP on one diagram, with **MP cutting AP at AP's peak** and MP going **below** the x-axis.
Keep the production function **physical**: no prices or costs.
slides.narration: Show your formulas before you calculate, and show each step. When marginal product falls but is still positive, total product rises at a diminishing rate; it does not fall. On diagrams, marginal product must cut average product at its highest point and can go below the axis. And keep the production function physical, without any prices.

decks.title: Production Function — Part 2: The Law of Variable Proportions and Returns to Scale
goals: State the Law of Variable Proportions with its assumptions
Explain the three stages with a diagram and their causes, and why a rational producer chooses Stage II
Explain the meaning of returns to scale and distinguish it from returns to a factor

slides.heading: Law of Variable Proportions and Returns to Scale
slides.body_md: Part 2 — what happens to output as more of **one input** is added to a **fixed** input, and what happens when **all inputs** grow together.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: the Law of Variable Proportions and its assumptions, the three stages, their causes, the rational producer and returns to scale
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we keep one factor fixed and keep adding another. What happens to output? The answer is one of the most important laws in economics, the Law of Variable Proportions. Then we let every factor change together and meet returns to scale.

slides.heading: The Law of Variable Proportions
slides.body_md:
As more units of a **variable factor** are combined with a **fixed factor**, the **marginal product** of the variable factor may **rise at first** but **eventually diminishes**, and may become **negative**.

It is also called the law of **returns to a factor**.

slides.narration: Here is the law. Keep adding units of a variable factor, such as workers, to a fixed factor, such as land. At first each extra worker may add more than the one before. But sooner or later each extra worker adds less, and if we go on, an extra worker may even reduce output. The proportion between the factors keeps changing, hence the name.

slides.heading: Assumptions of the law
bullets: **Technology** is unchanged.
**At least one factor is fixed.**
Units of the variable factor are **homogeneous** (equally efficient).
The period is **short**.

rows: Better methods would shift the whole TP curve
The law is about changing factor proportions
Units of the variable factor homogeneous

slides.heading: Why the stages happen
slides.body_md:
**Increasing returns:** fuller use of an **indivisible fixed factor**, **division of labour**.
**Diminishing returns:** the fixed factor becomes **scarce**; factors are **imperfect substitutes**.
**Negative returns:** **overcrowding** of the fixed factor.

rows: Fuller use of an indivisible fixed factor; division of labour
Fixed factor becomes scarce relative to the variable factor; factors are imperfect substitutes
Overcrowding and overuse of the fixed factor

visual.alt: Table of the causes of the three types of returns to a factor: increasing returns from fuller use of an indivisible fixed factor and division of labour; diminishing returns from scarcity of the fixed factor and imperfect substitution; negative returns from overcrowding

slides.narration: Why do the stages happen? At first, a big machine or a plot of land is under-used, and extra workers let it be used fully and let them specialise. Later the fixed factor becomes scarce compared with workers, and workers cannot fully replace land or machines. Finally, too many workers crowd the fixed factor and get in each other's way.

Step 2 — At 4.5 workers MP = AP: AP is highest.

slides.narration: Read the key points. At three workers marginal product is at its peak of twenty-seven quintals, so total product turns from rising faster to rising slower. At four and a half workers marginal product equals average product, so average product is highest. At six workers marginal product is zero and total product peaks at one hundred and eight quintals.

slides.heading: The rational producer chooses Stage II
slides.body_md: In **Stage III** fewer workers would give **more output**; in **Stage I** the fixed factor is **under-used**. So a rational producer operates in **Stage II**; the exact point depends on **prices**.

nodes.label: Stage I: AP of the variable factor still rising
Stage III: MP of the variable factor negative

visual.alt: Flow of the rational producer's choice: in Stage I it pays to add more of the variable factor, in Stage III it pays to use less, so the producer settles in Stage II
visual.caption: Why Stage II

slides.narration: Where should a sensible producer operate? Not in stage three, because there fewer workers would give more output at lower cost. Not in stage one, because there output per worker is still rising and the fixed factor is under-used, so it pays to add workers. So the producer works in stage two. Exactly where depends on wages and the price of output.

slides.heading: Returns to scale (meaning only)
slides.body_md:
**Returns to scale** describe how output changes when **all inputs** are changed in the **same proportion** in the **long run**.
- **Increasing:** output rises in a **greater** proportion.
- **Constant:** in the **same** proportion.
- **Diminishing:** in a **smaller** proportion.

slides.heading: Returns to a factor versus returns to scale
columns: **Returns to a factor:** short run, **one** input changes, factor proportion **changes**; increasing, diminishing and negative returns.
**Returns to scale:** long run, **all** inputs change together, proportion **unchanged**; increasing, constant and diminishing returns.

slides.narration: Do not mix the two ideas. Returns to a factor belong to the short run: one input changes and the proportion between factors changes. Returns to scale belong to the long run: every input changes in the same proportion, so the proportion stays the same. Their types also differ.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: State the law with **"fixed factor"**, **"variable factor"** and **"eventually"**.
Name each stage and say where it **ends**: AP maximum, then TP maximum (MP = 0).
Give **causes**, not just descriptions: indivisibility, scarcity of the fixed factor, overcrowding.
Rational producer: explain **why not Stage I** and **why not Stage III**.
Returns to scale: **meaning and three types only**; never confuse them with returns to a factor.
slides.narration: When you state the law, include the fixed factor, the variable factor and the word eventually. Name each stage and where it ends. Explain why the stages happen. For the rational producer, rule out stage one and stage three with reasons. And keep returns to scale to its meaning and three types.

notes.title: Production Function and Law of Variable Proportions — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The production function
sections.body_md:
A **production function** is the **technical relationship** between physical **inputs** and the **maximum physical output**, given **technology**: **Q = f(L, K)**.

- **Fixed factor:** cannot be changed in the period (plant, heavy machines).
- **Variable factor:** can be changed (labour, raw materials).

key_terms.definition_md: The technical relation between physical inputs and maximum physical output, for given technology.
An input whose quantity cannot be changed in the period considered.

visual.caption: Q = f(L, K)

sections.heading: 2. Short run and long run
sections.body_md:
- **Short run:** at least one factor fixed; output changes by changing the variable factor, so the **factor proportion changes**. This gives **returns to a factor**.
- **Long run:** **all factors variable**; inputs can change in the same proportion. This gives **returns to scale**.

sections.heading: 3. Total, average and marginal product
sections.body_md:
- **TP** = total output of the variable factor = **ΣMP**.
- **AP = TP ÷ L**.
- **MP = TPn − TPn−1** (= ΔTP ÷ ΔL).

Example: an imagined Nagpur packing shed packs 51 crates with 3 workers and 68 with 4, so the fourth worker's MP is 17 and AP with 4 workers is 17.

key_terms.definition_md: Output per unit of the variable factor, TP ÷ L.
The change in total product from one more unit of the variable factor.

sections.heading: 4. Relationships among TP, AP and MP
sections.body_md:
**TP and MP:** MP rising → TP rises at an increasing rate (to the **point of inflexion**); MP falling but positive → TP rises at a diminishing rate; **MP = 0 → TP maximum**; MP negative → TP falls.

**AP and MP:** MP > AP → AP rises; **MP = AP → AP maximum** (MP cuts AP at its peak); MP < AP → AP falls. MP can be negative; AP stays positive while TP is positive.

key_terms.definition_md: The point on the TP curve where it changes from rising at an increasing rate to rising at a diminishing rate; MP is maximum there.

sections.heading: 5. The Law of Variable Proportions and its stages
sections.body_md:
**Statement:** as more units of a variable factor are combined with a fixed factor, MP may rise at first but **eventually diminishes** and can become **negative**.

**Assumptions:** constant technology; at least one fixed factor; homogeneous units of the variable factor; short period.

**Stages** (convention used here): **I** — increasing returns, to the maximum of AP; **II** — diminishing returns, to the maximum of TP (MP = 0); **III** — negative returns. Some books end Stage I at the point of inflexion.

**Causes:** indivisibility of the fixed factor and division of labour; scarcity of the fixed factor and imperfect substitution; overcrowding.

**Rational producer:** operates in **Stage II**, where both factors have positive marginal products; the exact point depends on prices.

key_terms.definition_md: In the short run, the marginal product of a variable factor added to a fixed factor eventually diminishes.
The stage in which an extra unit of the variable factor reduces total product.

visual.alt: Table of the three stages of the Law of Variable Proportions: in Stage I total and average product rise and the stage ends where average product is maximum; in Stage II total product rises at a diminishing rate and marginal product falls to zero; in Stage III marginal product is negative and total product falls
visual.caption: Convention used here: Stage I ends at the maximum of AP.

sections.heading: 6. Returns to scale (meaning only)
sections.body_md:
**Returns to scale:** the response of output when **all inputs** change in the **same proportion** in the **long run**.
- **Increasing:** output rises more than in proportion.
- **Constant:** in the same proportion.
- **Diminishing:** less than in proportion.

Returns to scale differ from returns to a factor (short run, one input varied).

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that TP falls when MP falls; TP falls only when MP is negative.
- Drawing MP cutting AP anywhere other than AP's highest point.
- Saying AP becomes negative; only MP can.
- Explaining diminishing returns by "less efficient workers"; the law assumes homogeneous units.
- Mixing returns to a factor (short run, one input) with returns to scale (long run, all inputs).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: two points, or a calculation with its formula.
- 3 marks: three explained points, or a schedule with an interpretation.
- 5 marks: parts in order, with a described diagram and reasons.

questions.stem_md: For a firm, the production function shows the

options.text_md: relationship between the price of a good and the quantity of it produced
technical relationship between the physical quantities of inputs used and the maximum physical output obtained
money cost of producing each level of output
relationship between output and the profit the firm earns

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** technical relationship between the physical quantities of inputs used and the maximum physical output obtained. A production function is a purely technical, physical relation: given technology, it states the most output a set of inputs can produce. Prices, costs and profit are not part of it.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Sangli turmeric-grinding unit can hire extra helpers within a day but needs eighteen months to install a second grinding mill. In the short run, which input is the fixed factor?

options.text_md: The helpers
The raw turmeric
The electricity used each day
The grinding mill

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The grinding mill. A fixed factor is one whose quantity cannot be changed in the period considered. The mill cannot be added for eighteen months; helpers, turmeric and power can be varied quickly, so they are variable factors.

questions.stem_md: The long run, in the theory of production, is a period in which

options.text_md: all factors of production can be varied
at least one factor of production stays fixed
only labour can be changed
the firm cannot change its output at all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** all factors of production can be varied. In the long run every input, including plant and machinery, can be changed. A period with at least one fixed factor is the short run.

questions.stem_md: A Kanpur leather unit (imagined) studies how its daily output of bags changes as it adds cutters to its six fixed cutting tables. Which relationship is it studying?

options.text_md: A long-run production function, which leads to returns to scale
A cost function, which leads to average cost
A short-run production function, which leads to returns to a factor
A demand function, which leads to the law of demand

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A short-run production function, which leads to returns to a factor. Only one input (cutters) varies while the tables stay fixed: that is the short-run production function, whose behaviour is described by returns to a factor (the Law of Variable Proportions). Returns to scale need all inputs to vary.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A production function is stated in physical units of inputs and output, not in rupees.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** It links quantities of inputs (workers, machine-hours, kilograms of raw material) with a quantity of output; money values belong to cost and revenue analysis.

questions.stem_md: A factor whose quantity can be changed in the short run as output changes is called a ___ factor.
questions.solution_md: Labour and raw materials are usually variable factors; buildings and heavy machinery are fixed in the short run.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the short-run and the long-run production function, using an imagined Indian brick kiln.
questions.solution_md: One factor fixed versus all factors variable, with the kiln example.

answer.model_answer_md: In the **short-run** production function at least one factor is **fixed**: the kiln and its chimney stay the same while the owner adds **moulders**, so output changes only through the variable factor. In the **long-run** function **all factors can vary**: the owner can build a second kiln and change every input together.

marking_scheme.step: Short run: at least one fixed factor

questions.stem_md: For an imagined Bhagalpur silk-weaving shed, classify the looms, the shed, the weavers and the silk yarn as fixed or variable factors in the short run, with a reason.
questions.solution_md: Two fixed and two variable inputs, with the time-to-change reason.

answer.model_answer_md: The **looms** and the **shed** are **fixed**: they cannot be increased quickly. The **weavers** and the **silk yarn** are **variable**: the owner can hire more weavers or buy more yarn within days as output changes.

marking_scheme.step: Looms and shed fixed with reason
Weavers and yarn variable with reason

questions.stem_md: Marginal physical product of labour is the

options.text_md: total product divided by the number of workers
total output produced by all the workers together
change in total product when one more unit of labour is employed
output of the most efficient worker in the firm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** change in total product when one more unit of labour is employed. MP = TPn − TPn−1, the addition to total product from one more unit of the variable factor. TP ÷ L is average product.

questions.stem_md: A bakery in an imagined Shillong lane makes 160 loaves a day with 4 bakers and 185 loaves with 5 bakers, with the same oven. What is the marginal product of the fifth baker?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 25. MP of the fifth baker = 185 − 160 = 25 loaves. 37 is the average product with five bakers and 40 the average with four.

questions.stem_md: Total physical product of a variable factor reaches its maximum when the marginal product of that factor is

options.text_md: at its maximum
equal to average product
negative
zero

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** zero. TP keeps rising while MP is positive; it stops rising when the extra unit adds nothing (MP = 0) and falls once MP turns negative. So TP is at its maximum where MP is zero.

questions.stem_md: Average product of a variable factor is at its maximum where

options.text_md: marginal product is zero
marginal product equals average product
total product is at its maximum
marginal product is at its maximum

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** marginal product equals average product. When MP exceeds AP it pulls AP up; when MP is below AP it pulls AP down. AP therefore peaks where MP = AP: the MP curve cuts the AP curve at the top of AP.

questions.stem_md: Between the eighth and twelfth workers at an imagined Tirupur dyeing unit, total product keeps rising but each extra worker adds less than the one before. What is happening to marginal product?

options.text_md: It is falling but still positive
It is rising
It is zero
It is negative

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** It is falling but still positive. TP rising at a diminishing rate means each addition (MP) is smaller than the last but still adds output: MP is falling and positive. A negative MP would make TP fall.

questions.stem_md: Which of these statements about a firm producing positive output is correct?

options.text_md: Average product can become negative, but marginal product cannot
Marginal product can become negative, but average product cannot
Both can become negative at the same time
Neither can ever fall

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Marginal product can become negative, but average product cannot. AP = TP ÷ L stays positive as long as TP is positive. MP is the change in TP and turns negative when an extra worker reduces total output, for example through overcrowding.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined Moradabad brass unit, the marginal product of the next artisan is 14 vases while the average product so far is 11 vases. What happens to average product when this artisan joins?

options.text_md: It falls
It stays the same
It rises
It becomes zero

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It rises. An addition above the current average raises the average. Since MP (14) exceeds AP (11), AP rises.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Nagpur orange-packing shed packs 80 crates a day with 5 workers. What is the average product per worker at this level?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** 16. AP = TP ÷ L = 80 ÷ 5 = 16 crates. 12 would be the marginal product of the fifth worker.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When the sixth worker on an imagined Coorg coffee estate adds nothing to the day's picking, total product is at its maximum.

**Reason (R):** Total product rises as long as marginal product is positive and falls when marginal product is negative.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since TP rises while MP is positive and falls once it is negative, the point where MP is zero is where TP stops rising, its maximum.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At an imagined Hubli handloom unit, average product of weavers can keep rising for a while even after marginal product has started to fall.

**Reason (R):** Average product rises only while marginal product is itself rising.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: after MP peaks it falls but can still be above AP, and while MP exceeds AP the average keeps rising. R is false: what makes AP rise is MP being greater than AP, not MP rising.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Nagpur shed packs 51 crates a day with 3 workers and 68 with 4. Calculate the marginal product of the fourth worker.
questions.solution_md: MP = 68 − 51 = 17 crates.

questions.stem_md: On an imagined Thanjavur paddy plot the first five transplanting labourers add 6, 10, 13, 9, 5 rows a day respectively. Find total product with five labourers.
questions.solution_md: TP is the sum of the MPs: 6 + 10 + 13 + 9 + 5 = 43 rows.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Tiruppur tailoring unit has an average product of 8 shirts a day with 6 tailors. The seventh tailor's marginal product is 1 shirt. Find the average product with seven tailors.
questions.solution_md: TP with 6 tailors = 6 × 8 = 48. TP with 7 = 48 + 1 = 49. AP = 49 ÷ 7 = 7 shirts.

marking_scheme.step: TP with six and seven tailors

questions.stem_md: The imagined Shillong bakery makes 160 loaves a day with 4 bakers. What is the average product per baker?
questions.solution_md: AP = 160 ÷ 4 = 40 loaves.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The marginal product curve cuts the average product curve at the highest point of the average product curve.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** AP rises while MP is above it and falls once MP is below it, so the two meet where AP is at its peak.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Total product starts falling as soon as marginal product starts falling.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A falling but positive MP still adds to TP; TP only falls once MP becomes negative. MP falling first makes TP rise at a diminishing rate.

questions.stem_md: Match each behaviour of marginal product with what happens to total product at the imagined Nagpur packing shed.

options.text_md: MP rising
MP falling but positive
MP equal to zero
MP negative

match_right.text_md: TP rises at a diminishing rate
TP rises at an increasing rate

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). TP changes by the amount of MP each time, so the size and sign of MP decide how TP moves.

questions.stem_md: A floriculture farm near imagined Hosur produces 120 bouquets a week with one helper and 300 with two, with the same greenhouse. Calculate the marginal product and the average product of labour when two helpers are employed.
questions.solution_md: MP from the change in TP; AP from TP divided by workers.

answer.model_answer_md: **MP of the second helper** = 300 − 120 = **180 bouquets**. **AP with two helpers** = 300 ÷ 2 = **150 bouquets** per helper.

questions.stem_md: State the relationship between total product and marginal product when marginal product is (i) positive but falling and (ii) negative.
questions.solution_md: Two cases of the TP–MP link.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) When MP is **positive but falling**, TP **still rises**, but at a **diminishing rate**. (ii) When MP is **negative**, the extra unit reduces output, so TP **falls**.

questions.stem_md:
The total product of an imagined Nagpur orange-packing shed (one shed, workers variable) is given below. Calculate the marginal and average product for the first four workers and say how AP behaves while MP is above it.

| Workers | TP (crates a day) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 12 |
| 2 | 30 |
| 3 | 51 |
| 4 | 68 |
questions.solution_md: MP = change in TP; AP = TP ÷ workers; AP rises while MP > AP.

answer.model_answer_md: MP: **12, 18, 21, 17**. AP: **12, 15, 17, 17**. For the second and third workers MP (18, 21) is **above** AP, and AP **rises** (to 15 and 17); with the fourth worker MP (17) is equal to AP (17) and AP stops rising.

questions.stem_md: Explain three points of the relationship between average product and marginal product of a variable factor, with reference to a described diagram.
questions.solution_md: Three relationship points with the diagram.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. When **MP > AP**, AP **rises**: the MP curve lies **above** the AP curve.
2. When **MP = AP**, AP is at its **maximum**: MP cuts AP at the top of AP.
3. When **MP < AP**, AP **falls**; MP can even become **negative** while AP stays positive.

questions.stem_md: The marginal products of eight successive labourers transplanting paddy on an imagined Thanjavur plot are 6, 10, 13, 9, 5, 2, 0, -3 rows a day. Find total product at each level and identify where total product is at its maximum and where it falls.
questions.solution_md: Cumulative sum of MP; maximum where MP is zero; fall where MP is negative.

answer.model_answer_md: TP: **6, 16, 29, 38, 43, 45, 45, 42**. TP is **at its maximum (45 rows)** with the **sixth and seventh** labourers, where the seventh adds **zero**; with the **eighth** labourer MP is **negative (−3)** and TP **falls** to 42.

questions.stem_md: At an imagined Jodhpur bandhani (tie-dye) workshop with one dyeing vat, the marginal products of the first four dyers are 5, 9, 7, 3 dupattas a day. Find total and average product for each number of dyers and state what happens to average product when the fourth dyer joins, with the reason.
questions.solution_md: TP is the running sum of MP; AP = TP ÷ dyers; MP below AP pulls AP down.

answer.model_answer_md: Total product is the running sum of marginal products, so TP with one to four dyers is **5, 14, 21, 24** dupattas. Average product is TP divided by the number of dyers: **5, 7, 7, 6**. When the fourth dyer joins, **AP falls** from 7 to 6, because his **MP (3) is below the existing AP (7)**: an addition below the average always pulls the average down.

questions.stem_md: The Law of Variable Proportions states that, as more units of a variable factor are combined with a fixed factor,

options.text_md: output always rises in the same proportion as the variable factor
the marginal product of the variable factor keeps rising without limit
total product falls from the very first unit
the marginal product of the variable factor may rise at first but must eventually diminish

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the marginal product of the variable factor may rise at first but must eventually diminish. The law describes returns to a factor in the short run: MP may increase at first, but because the fixed factor does not grow, MP eventually diminishes and can become negative.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is an assumption of the Law of Variable Proportions?

options.text_md: All factors of production are increased together
Units of the variable factor differ in quality
The state of technology remains unchanged
The price of the product keeps rising

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The state of technology remains unchanged. The law assumes constant technology, at least one fixed factor, homogeneous units of the variable factor and a short period. Increasing all factors together is the subject of returns to scale.

questions.stem_md: In the third stage of the Law of Variable Proportions,

options.text_md: marginal product rises and total product rises at an increasing rate
marginal product of the variable factor is negative and total product falls
average product rises and marginal product is above it
marginal product is zero throughout

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** marginal product of the variable factor is negative and total product falls. Stage III begins once TP is at its maximum; beyond it each extra unit reduces output, so MP is negative and TP falls.

questions.stem_md: A rational producer prefers to operate in which stage of the Law of Variable Proportions?

options.text_md: Stage II
Stage I
Stage III
Any stage, since output is positive in all three

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Stage II. In Stage III fewer units of the variable factor would give more output, and in Stage I the fixed factor is under-used so adding the variable factor keeps raising its average output. Stage II, where both factors have positive marginal products, is where a rational producer operates.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Thrissur rubber estate keeps adding tappers to the same 400 trees. The main reason the marginal product of tappers eventually diminishes is that

options.text_md: the later tappers are always less skilled than the earlier ones
each tapper has fewer trees to work on, as the fixed factor does not grow
the price of rubber falls as more tappers are hired
the estate changes its technology after every new tapper

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** each tapper has fewer trees to work on, as the fixed factor does not grow. With a fixed number of trees, the fixed factor becomes scarce relative to the variable factor, so each extra tapper adds less. The law assumes homogeneous workers and constant technology, and prices play no part in it.

questions.stem_md: On a small fishing boat from an imagined Malvan harbour, adding a ninth crew member reduces the day's catch because the crew keep getting in each other's way. This is a case of

options.text_md: increasing returns to a factor (Stage I)
constant returns to scale
increasing returns to scale
negative returns to a factor (Stage III)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** negative returns to a factor (Stage III). A fall in total output from one more unit of the variable factor is negative marginal product, which marks Stage III. Overcrowding of the fixed factor (the boat) is its usual cause.

questions.stem_md: A big oil-expeller machine at an imagined Erode mill needs at least three operators to run properly; with one operator it runs only part of the day. Early increasing returns to operators here are best explained by

options.text_md: better use of an indivisible fixed factor as more operators are added
the fixed factor becoming scarce relative to the operators
overcrowding around the machine
a rise in the price of oil seeds

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** better use of an indivisible fixed factor as more operators are added. An indivisible fixed factor is under-used when few units of the variable factor work with it; adding operators uses it more fully and allows division of work, so marginal product rises at first.

questions.stem_md: A diagram of an imagined farm's production shows total product rising from 0 to its peak of 108 quintals at 6 workers and falling after that. With 7 workers, the marginal product of the last worker is

options.text_md: zero
positive and rising
negative
positive and falling

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** negative. Beyond the peak of TP each extra worker reduces output (TP falls from 108 to 98), so marginal product is negative.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A rational producer would never employ a variable factor in Stage III of the Law of Variable Proportions.

**Reason (R):** In Stage III the marginal product of the variable factor is negative, so withdrawing some units would raise total output.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true and R explains A: when the extra units actually reduce output, employing fewer of them would give more output at lower cost, so no rational producer stays in Stage III.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Law of Variable Proportions operates only in the short run.

**Reason (R):** In the long run a firm can change its technology.

Choose the correct option.

Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but R does not explain A. The law needs at least one fixed factor, which exists only in the short run; that is why it is a short-run law. Technology changing in the long run is a separate point (the law assumes constant technology anyway).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In Stage II of the Law of Variable Proportions, marginal product of the variable factor is falling but remains positive.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Stage II runs up to the point where TP is at its maximum (MP = 0); throughout it MP declines while staying positive, so TP rises at a diminishing rate.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these points on the marginal product curve of a variable factor in the order in which they occur as more units are added to a fixed factor.

options.text_md: MP becomes negative (TP falls)
MP reaches its maximum (point of inflexion of TP)
MP becomes zero (TP at its maximum)
MP becomes equal to AP (AP at its maximum)

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). MP peaks first; it then falls and cuts AP at AP's maximum; it reaches zero where TP peaks; finally it turns negative.

questions.stem_md: The point on the total product curve where it changes from rising at an increasing rate to rising at a diminishing rate is called the point of ___.
questions.solution_md: At the point of inflexion marginal product is at its maximum; after it TP rises at a diminishing rate.

questions.stem_md: State any two assumptions of the Law of Variable Proportions.
questions.solution_md: Any two correct assumptions.

answer.model_answer_md: 1. The **state of technology is constant**. 2. **At least one factor is fixed** while only the variable factor changes (and all units of the variable factor are **homogeneous**).

questions.stem_md: Explain why an imagined Bikaner wool-carding shed with four carding machines would never knowingly employ so many workers that it enters Stage III.
questions.solution_md: Negative MP: fewer workers give more output at less cost.

answer.model_answer_md: In **Stage III** each extra worker makes **total output fall** (negative MP), for example because workers crowd the four machines. The shed would get **more output with fewer workers**, so paying for them would only **raise cost and cut output**.

marking_scheme.step: Irrational to pay for output-reducing workers

questions.stem_md: Describe the behaviour of total, average and marginal product in Stage II of the Law of Variable Proportions.
questions.solution_md: Behaviour of TP, AP and MP in Stage II.

answer.model_answer_md: **TP** rises at a **diminishing rate** and reaches its **maximum** at the end of the stage. **AP** **falls** after its peak. **MP** **falls** and becomes **zero** at the end of the stage, staying below AP.

questions.stem_md: Explain the three stages of the Law of Variable Proportions in terms of what happens to marginal and total product in each stage.
questions.solution_md: Three stages with MP and TP behaviour.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Stage I (increasing returns to the factor):** MP **rises** at first and stays **above AP**, so **AP rises**; TP rises, at first at an increasing rate.
2. **Stage II (diminishing returns):** MP **falls** but stays **positive**; TP rises at a **diminishing rate** to its **maximum**, where MP = 0.
3. **Stage III (negative returns):** MP is **negative** and TP **falls**.

questions.stem_md: Using an imagined Ratnagiri cashew-processing unit with one roasting drum, explain one cause each of increasing, diminishing and negative returns to the variable factor.
questions.solution_md: One cause per type of return, tied to the drum.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Increasing returns:** the drum is **indivisible** and under-used by one or two workers; more workers use it **fully** and **divide the work** (feeding, roasting, shelling).
2. **Diminishing returns:** once the drum is fully used it becomes **scarce** relative to workers, so each extra worker adds **less**.
3. **Negative returns:** too many workers **crowd** around the one drum and **get in each other's way**, so output falls.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate the claim that a rational producer will operate only in Stage II of the Law of Variable Proportions.
questions.solution_md: Reasons to leave Stages III and I; Stage II with the exact point set by prices.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. In **Stage III** the variable factor has a **negative** MP: withdrawing some units **raises output and cuts cost**, so the producer moves back.
2. In **Stage I** AP of the variable factor is still **rising** and the fixed factor is **under-used**, so it pays to **add** more of the variable factor.
3. So the producer settles in **Stage II**, where both factors have **positive** MP; the **exact point** depends on **factor and product prices**. The claim is **valid**.

marking_scheme.step: Conclusion on Stage II with price point

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the Law of Variable Proportions and its assumptions. [2]
(b) Explain its three stages with the help of a described TP, AP and MP diagram. [3]
questions.solution_md: Statement and assumptions; three stages located on the diagram.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) As more units of a **variable factor** are combined with a **fixed factor**, the **marginal product** of the variable factor may **rise at first** but **eventually diminishes** and may become **negative**. Assumptions: **constant technology**, at least **one fixed factor**, **homogeneous** units of the variable factor, a **short period**.
(b) With labour on the x-axis and output on the y-axis: **Stage I** runs from the origin to the point where **AP is at its maximum** (MP cuts AP); TP rises, first at an increasing rate. **Stage II** runs to the point where **TP is at its maximum** and **MP is zero**; MP and AP fall. **Stage III** lies beyond: **MP is negative** and TP falls.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain the relationship between total product and marginal product with a described diagram. [3]
(b) Explain the relationship between average product and marginal product. [2]
questions.solution_md: Four TP–MP cases with the diagram; three AP–MP cases.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **MP rising** → TP rises at an **increasing rate** (up to the point of **inflexion**, where MP is at its maximum). **MP falling but positive** → TP rises at a **diminishing rate**. **MP = 0** → TP is at its **maximum**. **MP negative** → TP **falls**. On the diagram the TP curve is steepest where MP peaks and flat at its top where MP crosses the x-axis.
(b) **MP > AP** → AP **rises**; **MP = AP** → AP is at its **maximum**; **MP < AP** → AP **falls**. MP can become **negative**; AP stays positive while TP is positive.

marking_scheme.step: AP falling; MP negative while AP positive

questions.stem_md:
An imagined Thanjavur farmer records the marginal product of each extra transplanting labourer on a two-acre plot: 6, 10, 13, 9, 5, 2, 0, -3 rows a day.
(a) Calculate total product and average product for each number of labourers. [3]
(b) Using the marginal products, explain where total product stops rising, and advise the farmer how many labourers to hire if each costs the same and his only aim is not to waste labour. [2]
questions.solution_md: Cumulative TP; AP = TP ÷ L; advice from MP reaching zero.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Total product is the running sum of the marginal products: **6, 16, 29, 38, 43, 45, 45, 42** rows a day for one to eight labourers. Average product is TP divided by the number of labourers: **6, 8, 9.667, 9.5, 8.6, 7.5, 6.429, 5.25** rows.
(b) TP keeps rising while MP is positive and stops rising at **45 rows** with **6 labourers**: the **seventh adds zero** (TP stays at 45, its maximum) and the **eighth reduces** output because his MP is **−3**, so TP falls to 42. He should hire **no more than 6 labourers**. A seventh labourer would cost a wage and add nothing, and an eighth would actually lower the day's work, so both would waste labour on a fixed plot.

questions.stem_md: An imagined salt-pan owner in the Little Rann of Kutch keeps the same 20-acre pan and adds more salt workers each season. Explain why the Law of Variable Proportions applies here, naming the fixed and the variable factor and describing what happens to the marginal product of workers.
questions.solution_md: Fixed land, variable labour; MP rises, then diminishes, possibly negative.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **salt pan (land)** is the **fixed factor** and the **workers** are the **variable factor**, so only the **factor proportion** changes: this is the **short-run** situation the law describes.
2. At first more workers use the pan **more fully** (raking, carrying, heaping), so **MP rises**.
3. As workers increase on the same pan, each has **less land to work**, so **MP diminishes** and, if the pan is overcrowded, can become **negative**.

marking_scheme.step: Fixed and variable factors with short run

questions.stem_md:
A described diagram for an imagined Bastar millet farm (fixed land, workers variable) shows: marginal product reaches its highest value of 27 quintals at 3 workers; average product reaches its highest value of 20.25 quintals at 4.5 workers on the smooth curve; total product reaches its highest value of 108 quintals at 6 workers.
(a) What happens to the total product curve at 3 workers, what is the marginal product at 4.5 workers, and what is the marginal product at 6 workers? Give a reason for each. [3]
(b) Identify the range of workers that lies in Stage III, and explain why the farmer should never employ workers in it. [2]
questions.solution_md: Inflexion at MP maximum; MP = AP at AP maximum; MP = 0 at TP maximum; Stage III beyond TP maximum.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) At **3 workers** MP is at its **maximum**, so the TP curve reaches its **point of inflexion**: it stops rising at an increasing rate and starts rising at a **diminishing** rate. At **4.5 workers** AP is at its maximum, so **MP = AP = 20.25** quintals, because MP cuts AP at AP's peak. At **6 workers** TP is at its maximum, so **MP = 0**: the last worker adds nothing.
(b) **Stage III** is **more than 6 workers**, where MP is **negative** and TP **falls**. Employing them would mean paying wages for workers who **reduce** output, so the farmer should never do it.

the price of the product changes

only the fixed factor is reduced

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** all factors of production are changed in the same proportion in the long run. Returns to scale are a long-run idea: every input is changed by the same proportion. Changing one factor with others fixed is returns to a factor.

options.text_md: increasing returns to scale
constant returns to scale

A: returns to a factor; B: returns to scale
Both: returns to a factor
Both: returns to scale

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Returns to scale need every input, including the building, to change in the same proportion, which is possible only in the long run.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The imagined Ankleshwar paint plant shows increasing returns to scale because its output doubled when all inputs doubled.

**Reason (R):** Returns to scale are measured by changing only one input while keeping the others fixed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are false. Output doubling when all inputs double is constant returns to scale, not increasing. And returns to scale change all inputs together; changing one input is returns to a factor.

questions.stem_md: Define increasing, constant and diminishing returns to scale.
questions.solution_md: Three proportion-based definitions.

answer.model_answer_md: When all inputs rise in the same proportion, output rises in a **greater proportion** (**increasing**), the **same proportion** (**constant**) or a **smaller proportion** (**diminishing**) returns to scale.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between returns to a factor and returns to scale on the basis of time period and factor proportions.
questions.solution_md: Short run and changing proportion versus long run and constant proportion.

answer.model_answer_md: **Returns to a factor** are a **short-run** idea: only **one factor** varies, so the **factor proportion changes**. **Returns to scale** are a **long-run** idea: **all factors** change in the **same proportion**, so the **factor proportion stays the same**.

questions.stem_md:
Three imagined factories each doubled all their inputs. Identify the type of returns to scale for each, showing the percentage change in output.

| Factory | Output before | Output after doubling inputs |

| Kolhapur sugar mill | 400 | 960 |

1. **Kolhapur sugar mill:** output rises **140 per cent** against inputs **100 per cent** → **increasing returns to scale**.
2. **Ankleshwar paint plant:** output rises **100 per cent** against inputs **100 per cent** → **constant returns to scale**.
3. **Ludhiana cycle-parts unit:** output rises **60 per cent** against inputs **100 per cent** → **diminishing returns to scale**.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between the short-run and the long-run production function, giving an example of a fixed and a variable factor for an imagined Agra marble-cutting unit. [2]
(b) Explain the meaning of returns to scale and its three types, and state how they differ from returns to a factor. [3]
questions.solution_md: Short versus long run with examples; meaning and types of returns to scale; contrast.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In the **short run** at least one factor is **fixed** (the **cutting machines** and shed), while **workers and marble blocks** are **variable**. In the **long run** **all factors** can change, including the number of machines and the size of the shed.
(b) **Returns to scale** show how output responds when **all inputs** change in the **same proportion** in the long run: **increasing** (output rises more than in proportion), **constant** (same proportion) and **diminishing** (less than in proportion). **Returns to a factor** concern **one** input changing with others **fixed**, in the short run.

marking_scheme.step: Short run with fixed and variable examples
Contrast with returns to a factor

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain the causes of increasing and diminishing returns to a variable factor. [3]
(b) An imagined Kochi seafood-processing unit with one freezer finds that its tenth packer reduces output. Should it keep this packer? Justify your answer using the stages of production. [2]
questions.solution_md: Causes of increasing and diminishing returns; Stage III decision.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Increasing returns:** fuller use of an **indivisible fixed factor** and **division of labour** among more workers raise each worker's addition to output. **Diminishing returns:** once the fixed factor is fully used it becomes **scarce** relative to the variable factor, and factors are **imperfect substitutes**, so each extra worker adds less.
(b) **No.** A tenth packer who **reduces output** has a **negative marginal product**: the unit is in **Stage III**. Removing him would **raise output and cut cost**, so a rational producer moves back into **Stage II**.

marking_scheme.step: Negative MP and Stage III identified

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts about an imagined Shillong bakery with one oven. [2 + 2]

(i) It makes 160 loaves a day with 4 bakers and 185 with 5. Calculate the marginal product of the fifth baker and the average product with five bakers.
(ii) The owner says a sixth baker would add fewer loaves than the fifth. Name the tendency she expects and give its cause.
questions.solution_md: MP and AP calculations; diminishing returns with cause.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **MP** of the fifth baker = 185 − 160 = **25 loaves**; **AP** with five bakers = 185 ÷ 5 = **37 loaves** per baker.
(ii) She expects **diminishing returns to a factor** (diminishing marginal product). The **oven is fixed**, so each extra baker has **less oven space and time** to work with; the fixed factor becomes **scarce** relative to bakers, and bakers cannot fully replace the missing oven capacity, so each new baker adds fewer loaves than the one before.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 2]

(i) Explain what happens to marginal product and average product in Stage I of the Law of Variable Proportions, and why the stage gets its name.
(ii) A manager of an imagined Panipat blanket mill wants to stop hiring as soon as marginal product starts falling. Advise her, with a reason.
questions.solution_md: Stage I behaviour and name; advice to continue into Stage II.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) In **Stage I**, **MP rises** at first and stays **above AP**, so **AP keeps rising**; it is called the stage of **increasing returns** to the factor because output per worker increases.
(ii) She should **not stop** there. A falling but **positive MP** still **adds to output**, and **AP is still rising** while MP is above it; the mill should keep adding workers into **Stage II**, stopping at a point set by wages and prices, and certainly **before MP becomes negative**.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [2 + 2]

(i) An imagined Ankleshwar paint plant doubled every input and its output went from 250 to 500 litres a day. Name the type of returns to scale and explain.
(ii) Explain why this observation tells us nothing about the Law of Variable Proportions for the same plant.
questions.solution_md: Constant returns from equal proportions; why returns to scale differ from the law.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Constant returns to scale**: inputs rose by **100 per cent** and output also by **100 per cent**, the **same proportion**.
(ii) The Law of Variable Proportions concerns changing **one input** while **others stay fixed** in the **short run**; here **all inputs** changed together in the **long run**, so the **factor proportion did not change** and the law is not being tested.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) An imagined Nagpur orange-packing shed records total product with 1 to 8 workers: 12, 30, 51, 68, 80, 84, 84, 80 crates a day. Calculate the marginal product of every worker and the average product with 2, 4 and 6 workers.
(ii) Explain, using the relationships between TP, AP and MP, why the shed's manager stopped hiring at 6 workers when wages were high, and why the 8th worker should never have been hired.
questions.solution_md: MP and AP computed; hiring decision explained by the stages and the curves.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **MP** is the change in TP for each extra worker: **12, 18, 21, 17, 12, 4, 0, -4** crates. **AP** is TP divided by workers: with 2 workers **15**, with 4 **17**, with 6 **14** crates.
(ii) Up to the fourth worker MP is at or above AP, so AP rises. After the 4th worker MP falls **below** AP, so **AP falls** and each worker produces less on average. The **6th worker adds only 4 crates**; when wages are high, a worker adding so little is **not worth his wage**, so the manager stops hiring there, inside **Stage II**, where MP is still positive but small. The **7th worker adds zero**, so TP is at its **maximum** of 84 crates, and the **8th has a negative MP (-4)**: output **falls** to 80, which is **Stage III**. Paying a worker whose presence **reduces** total output can never be rational, so the 8th worker should never have been hired.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain the concept of a production function and distinguish between its short-run and long-run forms with an imagined Indian example.
(ii) A company plans to build a second, identical mill beside its first in an imagined Kolhapur district and expects output to more than double. Evaluate this expectation using the idea of returns to scale.
questions.solution_md: Concept and forms of the production function; balanced evaluation of returns to scale.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) A **production function** is the **technical relationship** between **physical inputs** and the **maximum physical output**, given **technology**: Q = f(L, K). In the **short run** at least one input is **fixed** (an imagined Sivakasi printing press cannot add machines within weeks, only workers), so output changes through the **variable factor** and returns to a factor apply. In the **long run** **all inputs** can change, and **returns to scale** apply.
(ii) Output **more than doubling** would mean **increasing returns to scale**. This is possible if the larger operation allows **specialised machines**, **bulk buying** of cane and **better division of work**. But an **identical** second mill doing the same as the first would more likely give **constant returns** (output just doubles), and problems of **management and coordination** could even give **diminishing returns**. The expectation is **optimistic**: it holds only if the bigger scale brings real **gains in organisation**.
